q: A population has N = 16 equally likely outcomes. A two-way table has row totals C = 6, D = 10 and column totals A = 9, B = 7. Let y be the count in the A∩C cell. What must y be for A and C to be mutually exclusive?
e: Mutually exclusive means the two events share no outcomes at all — A∩C is empty. An empty cell holds 0 outcomes, whatever the totals are. The totals never enter this one; that is what separates it from independence.

q: Same table: N = 16, row totals C = 6, D = 10, column totals A = 9, B = 7. What must y (the A∩C count) be for A and C to be independent?
e: Independent means P(A∩C) = P(A)·P(C). With equally likely outcomes every probability is a count over N, so y/16 = (9/16)·(6/16), giving y = 9·6/16 = 27/8. Notice this is almost never 0. Mutually exclusive and independent are different conditions, and two events that both have probability above 0 cannot be both at once.

q: You are proving P(Aᶜ|B) = 1 − P(A|B). Starting from the definition, P(Aᶜ|B) = P(Aᶜ∩B)/P(B). What is the next move?
o: Split B into the part inside A and the part outside: B = (A∩B) ∪ (Aᶜ∩B)
Assume A and B are independent
e: Every outcome in B is either also in A or not in A — there is no third option. So B is the union of two pieces that do not overlap, and the probability of B is the sum of their probabilities. That is the only fact the proof needs.

q: In that proof, why can you write P(B) = P(A∩B) + P(Aᶜ∩B) as a sum?
o: Because A and B are independent
The two pieces are disjoint, and probability adds over disjoint sets
e: Disjoint means no outcome is in both pieces. An outcome in B is either in A or outside A, never both, so the two pieces cover B without overlapping. Probability is additive exactly on sets that do not overlap — that is one of the axioms, not something you derive.

q: 80% of students who enroll complete the program. Of those who complete it, 65% attend the optional review sessions. Of those who do not complete it, 90% do not attend the review sessions. A randomly selected student attended the review sessions. What is the probability they completed the program?
e: You are asked for P(complete | review), but you were handed P(review | complete). Bayes' theorem flips a conditional probability around. Top: P(review and complete) = 0.65·0.8 = 0.52. Bottom: everyone who attends, from either group — 0.65·0.8 + 0.1·0.2 = 0.54. Note the 90% was for not attending, so the rate you need is 1 − 0.9 = 0.1. Divide: 0.963.

q: Same setup — complete: 80%; review given complete: 65%; no review given not complete: 90%. What fraction of all enrolled students attend the review sessions?
e: The law of total probability: split the population by whether they complete, work out the attendance rate inside each group, then weight each by how big the group is. 0.65·0.8 + 0.1·0.2 = 0.54. This is the denominator Bayes' theorem needs, which is why it is worth computing on its own.

q: An urn holds 8 blue, 15 red and 8 green balls. Three are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability all three are the same colour?
e: 'All the same colour' means all blue, or all red, or all green — three outcomes that cannot happen together, so add them. Choosing 3 from 8 blue can be done C(8,3) = 56 ways; likewise 455 and 56, giving 567. All possible draws: C(31,3) = 4495. So 567/4495 = 0.12614. Order does not matter here, which is why these are combinations and not permutations.

q: A coin is flipped until the first heads. X is the number of flips, counting the one that lands heads. The claim is P(X = x) = (1/2)ˣ for x = 1, 2, 3, … To show this is a valid probability mass function — a rule assigning probability to each value — what two things must you check?

q: Still with P(X = x) = (1/2)ˣ for x = 1, 2, 3, … What does ∑ (1/2)ˣ from x = 1 to ∞ equal?

q: An experiment succeeds with probability 1/6 on each trial, independently. In 15 trials, what is the probability of at least one success?

q: A continuous random variable has density f(x) = c·x^2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 4, and 0 elsewhere. What is c?
e: A density has to enclose total area 1. ∫₀^4 c·x^2 dx = c·4^3/3, so setting that equal to 1 gives c = 3/4^3 = 3/64. For a continuous variable the area is the probability — the height f(x) is not a probability and can be bigger than 1.

q: For a continuous random variable X, what is P(X = 3) exactly?

q: P(X = x) = x/10 for x = 1, 2, 3, 4. Is this a valid probability mass function?
o: Yes — all values are ≥ 0 and they sum to 1
No — a pmf must be decreasing
No — the values are not equal
e: Add them: (1 + 2 + 3 + 4)/10 = 10/10 = 1, and none is negative. That is both conditions, so it is valid. A pmf does not have to be flat, decreasing, or any particular shape.

q: P(X = x) = c/3ˣ for x = 1, 2, 3, … What must c be?
e: ∑ (1/3)ˣ from x = 1 is (1/3)/(1 − 1/3) = 1/2. For the total to be 1 you need c·(1/2) = 1, so c = 2. The series starting at x = 1 rather than x = 0 is what makes it 1/2 and not 3/2.

q: A classmate writes P(X = x) = (1/2)ˣ for x = 0, 1, 2, … What is wrong with it?
o: It is only valid for x ≥ 1 integers
e: Starting the sum at x = 0 adds a first term of 1, giving 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + … = 2. A pmf has to total exactly 1, so the index has to start at 1. An off-by-one in the starting index is the usual way this goes wrong.

q: For a continuous X, how do P(X < 2) and P(X ≤ 2) compare?
o: P(X ≤ 2) is larger by a small amount
e: They differ only by P(X = 2), and for a continuous variable that is 0. So the ≤ and < versions always agree. For a discrete variable they do not, which is why the distinction matters there and not here.

q: A density f(x) takes the value 2.5 at some point. Is that a problem?
o: Yes — the density must stay below 1
Only if the range is wider than 1
No — a density is a height, and only the area has to total 1
e: The constraint is on area, not height. A variable uniform on [0, 0.4] has density 2.5 everywhere, and its total area is still 2.5 × 0.4 = 1. Heights above 1 are normal when the range is narrow.

q: N = 20 equally likely outcomes. A two-way table has A∩C = y, B∩C = 7, A∩D = 3, and B∩D = z, totalling 20. For what value(s) of y are A and C independent?
e: Independence is P(A∩C) = P(A)·P(C), and here y appears in the totals as well as the cell. Row C totals y+7; column A totals y+3. So y/20 = ((y+3)/20)·((y+7)/20), which clears to 20y = (y+3)(y+7) — a quadratic, not a one-step division. Solving gives y = 3 or 7, and both satisfy the table. The question asks for value(s): give every root that keeps all four cells at zero or above.

So y/30 = ((y+5)/30)·((y+4)/30), which clears to 30y = (y+5)(y+4) — a quadratic, not a one-step division. Solving gives y = 1 or 20, and both satisfy the table. The question asks for value(s): give every root that keeps all four cells at zero or above.
